articles.title: Google Disrupts Massive Android TV Botnet Exploiting Firmwares
articles.content: Google and an assortment of partners shut down a botnet that an approved Android device manufacturer purposefully deployed across more than 1.3 million TV set-top boxes, the company said Monday.  Videostrong Technology Co., a China-based Android original equipment and device manufacturer, implanted a backdoor into multiple devices it sold. Those backdoors established XCPE, an expansive botnet that cybercriminals used to conduct ad fraud, steal data and route malicious traffic through residential proxy networks, according to a Google Threat Intelligence Group report. Google took legal action to shut down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet. The company also took down command-and-control domains that more than a dozen malware families ran as modules through the XCPE backdoor, claiming it disrupted access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices from various manufacturers. Videostrong sold Android devices with pre-installed malware for years, slipping by Google’s security tests by loading the malicious code after the device’s first boot. “The XCPE operators constantly evolved its configurations to evade Google’s pre and post-launch detections,” Charley Snyder, head of disruption operations at GTIG, told CyberScoop. Snyder declined to say when or how Google first became aware of the approved vendor running a botnet on Android-powered devices.  “We found this malicious software built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years, supported by dedicated infrastructure and constantly evolving configurations to evade detection and manage their affiliates,” Google researchers wrote in the report. “We believe this campaign wasn’t an isolated rogue insider or a development oversight.” Google banned Videostrong and any future subsidiaries from building or selling certified Android devices, and said it changed its review process to detect and stop similar activities in the future. Yet, Snyder said the company isn’t sharing specifics on these changes because it doesn’t want to provide threat actors insights that might help them circumvent these additional protections. Most of the devices comprising the XCPE botnet were Android TV set-top boxes, but researchers also observed infected Android-based telehealth devices, karaoke machines and digital signs.  “Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors,” researchers wrote in the report. “This led to a variety of malicious activities being conducted on and through the devices, including ad-fraud, data exfiltration, and routing malicious network traffic through the devices.” The botnet spanned more than 170 countries , with the largest concentration of infected devices based in Malaysia, Brazil, Iraq, Mexico and Taiwan, according to TrendAI researchers. Nearly 44,000 infected devices were based in the United States between June and October. Google also partnered with Japan’s National Police Agency, Lumen Technologies , Human Security, Plume and Synthient to study and disrupt the botnet.  The company said the dismantling of XCPE “seriously impacted over a dozen malicious actors,” yet it warned that the underlying market for backdoors, ad fraud and residential proxy networks are resilient and operating as an interconnected supply chain.

articles.title: Defense Sector Demands Renewal of Cyber Threat Sharing
articles.content: Stay Connected Featured eBooks Health Technology: Relaunch of VA EHR Read Now Law Enforcement Technology Read Now Insights & Reports By David DiMolfetta , Cybersecurity Reporter, Nextgov/FCW | November 2, 2026 05:17 PM ET Banks, utilities and other industries want lawmakers to extend liability protections through 2035. A stopgap measure currently keeps them in place until Dec. 11. Congress Industry Cyber Defense A coalition of 35 industry groups is urging Congress to use the annual defense policy bill to renew a law that gives companies legal protections when they share information about cyber threats with the federal government. In a Nov. 1 letter to the leaders of the House and Senate Armed Services committees, the groups asked negotiators to keep a provision in the House bill that would extend the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015 through 2035. The law lapsed during last year’s record government shutdown and has since stayed in place through a series of spending bills. Its current extension expires Dec. 11. The signers include the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, Business Software Alliance, American Bankers Association, Airlines for America, the American Public Power Association and the National Rural Water Association. “In this environment, the speed and breadth with which defenders share information determines whether they keep pace with adversaries,” the groups wrote. “That speed depends on the legal certainty CISA 2015 provides.” The key liability protections in the law are designed to shield firms from lawsuits and regulatory penalties when sharing threat information with federal partners like the FBI or National Security Agency. That data often includes personal or proprietary information tied to individuals and companies affected in cyber intrusions. Industry groups have consistently warned lawmakers that allowing the measure to lapse would create legal risks for companies sharing breach data, leading to a drop in private sector threat disclosures. On the first day of the shutdown last year, cybersecurity attorneys were already fielding calls from clients about whether their existing agreements still protected them. Congress restored the law through January 2026, when it reopened the government in November 2025. Lawmakers extended it again in February of this year, this time through Sept. 30, then moved the deadline to December in a stopgap funding bill. A sticking point in the Senate reauthorization process has been what else to put in a longer renewal. Sens. Gary Peters, D-Mich., and Mike Rounds, R-S.D., pushed for a 10-year extension during last year’s shutdown. But Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., told Roll Call last month that he wanted a provision barring federal officials from pressuring social media companies to restrict speech. Paul — who has routinely pushed back on clean extensions of the law — said he and Peters had discussed the amendment several times without reaching an agreement. Share This:

articles.title: Police Dismantle Botnet Exploiting 1.3 Million Android Streaming Devices
articles.content: Videostrong accused of shipping devices with a backdoor baked in Jessica Lyons Jessica Lyons Cybersecurity Editor Published mon 2 Nov 2026 // 19:03 UTC Make us preferred on Google Max-severity bug in widely used OT programming tool exploited to deliver Linux malware now Thieves pilfer environment variables from Trigger AI workflow tool 6 hours ago Token thieves costing companies $100K+ per day in illicit LLM charges 6 hours ago Nuclear threats and street brawls: Russia, Ukraine report attacks on their emergency alert apps 8 hours ago Frozen part II: Hackers remotely defrost produce in Euro supermarkets ... again 9 hours ago A coalition of private-sector security firms working with Japan’s National Police Agency has disrupted XCPE, a backdoor used to build a massive botnet comprising more than 1.3 million Android devices across more than 200 countries. Google, Lumen, Human Security, Plume, Synthient, and TrendAI participated in the disruption. “We assess with high confidence that the backdoor and botnet were intentionally developed, deployed, and operated for financial gain by Videostrong Technology,” the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said in a Monday blog. Videostrong Technology is a hardware manufacturer based in Shenzhen, China. It builds Android devices, including home TV boxes and projectors. According to Google, Videostrong deliberately embedded the XCPE backdoor in device firmware and sold access to criminal affiliates , allowing them to install additional malware modules on devices shipped to unsuspecting customers. When buyers connected these devices to their home networks, the preinstalled backdoor allowed operators to create proxy networks and hide malicious traffic using the customers' internet connections without their knowledge. The firmware’s pre-installed management agent purported to be a standard remote-management client, according to TrendAI. It pulled updates from a GitHub page, and connected to a Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT) server that gave the operator full remote control of each box, allowing them to install and remove apps, change settings, and push updates to the infected devices. Between June 3 and October 1, TrendAI documented more than 3.8 million distinct home and mobile IP addresses connected to the operation. The coalition also disrupted the command-and-control domains used to manage the affiliate modules. “Because these affiliates each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE, we assess that taking down their C2 domains will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices,” according to GTIG.  Google said it had since cut ties with Videostrong, and banned the OEM from making devices with preloaded Google apps.  Videostrong did not immediately respond to The Register’ s inquiries. This backdoor and botnet operation is part of the same ecosystem as BadBox 2.0 , another notorious botnet that infected more than 10 million TV boxes and other devices before Human, Google, and TrendAI  disrupted it in March 2025.® cyber-crime botnet android google security Make us preferred on Google

articles.content: 본문 사회일반 ‘인플루언서와 만남’ 빙자 17억 뜯어내…태국 거점 피싱 조직 송치 정봉비 기자 수정 2026-11-03 11:03 펼침 0:00 Your browser does not support the audio element. 한겨레 자료 인플루언서 등과의 조건만남을 빙자해 단계별 추가 비용 명목으로 17억여원을 뜯어낸 태국 거점 보이스피싱 조직원들이 공소청에 넘겨졌다. 서울 송파경찰서는 태국 방콕에 거점을 둔 보이스피싱 범죄단체 조직원 9명을 범죄단체가입·활동 및 통신사기피해환급법 위반 혐의로 구속 송치했다고 3일 밝혔다. 공범인 조직원 1명과 범행에 쓰인 대포(차명)계좌 명의자 14명도 함께 불구속 송치됐다. 이들은 지난해 8월부터 올해 6월까지 허위 성매매 누리집을 통해 연락해 온 피해자들에게 ‘조건만남 진행시 보안 인증 등 추가 비용이 필요하다’고 속여 돈을 뜯어낸 혐의를 받는다. 현재까지 확인된 피해자는 11명(피해액 약 5억원)이지만, 범행 계좌 분석 결과 전체 피해 규모는 17억7000여만원에 달하는 것으로 추산된다. 경찰 조사에 따르면 이들은 캄보디아, 베트남을 거쳐 태국으로 거점을 옮겨 방콕의 한 4층 빌라 전체를 임차해 피싱범죄 콜센터 장소로 활용했다. 이들은 피해자에게 가입비, 만남 예약금 등을 명목으로 일정 금액을 받아낸 뒤, 만남 전 거쳐야하는 절차 명목으로 보안심의 등을 요구하며 각 단계별로 금액을 올려가며돈을 요구한 것으로 조사됐다. 한 피해자는 데이트 매칭 가입비로 2만원을 입금한 뒤 예약 보증금, 보안 인증비, 시스템 복구비 등 총 16차례에 걸쳐 1억5천880만원을 빼앗겼다고 한다. 태국 방콕에 거점을 둔 보이스피싱 범죄 단체가 교육, 활용용으로 공유했던 시나리오. 서울 송파경찰서 제공 이들 조직은 피해자를 속이기 위한 치밀한 시나리오도 준비했다. 가령 피해자가 돈을 받는 이유를 물으면 “(만남 여성이) 인플루언서, 모델, 연습생 같은 신분 노출을 꺼려하시는 분들이 대부분이라 보안상 받는다”고 하거나 “3일째부터 ‘우리 근데 언제 봐?’ 이런 식으로 매칭 뒤 만남을 유도해주셔야 한다”는 식으로 입금을 유도하는 방식이었다. 뜯어낸 금액 중 일부를 돌려주며 피해자를 안심시키기도 했다. 경찰청 국제치안협력국은 지난 6월 국정원과 송파경찰서에서 현지 조직 정보를 입수한 뒤 태국 경찰과 합동 작전을 벌여 피의자들을 검거했다. 경찰 관계자는 “온라인에서 접촉한 불상의 상대가 가입비, 수수료 등의 명목으로 송금을 요구하면 일단 피싱범죄로 의심해야 한다”며 “의심이 들 경우 초기에 과감히 단절하고 의심스러운 전화나 에스엔에스 대화는 즉시 종료할 것을 당부했다. 정봉비 기자 bee@hani.co.kr

articles.title: Corporate Giants Lobby Congress To Shield Private Cyber Threat Sharing
articles.content: Major industry groups are clamoring for Congress to include a 10-year extension of a law that they say is essential to cyber threat information sharing in the annual defense policy bill. Congress has mixed a series of short-term renewals and lapses of the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015 (CISA 2015) — which provides legal protections for threat data exchanges between the government and private sector as well as between companies — since its previous 10-year sunset came and went last year. It’s now set to expire again on Dec. 11 . On Sunday, 35 business groups sent a letter to leaders of the House and Senate Armed Services panels, asking them to renew the law for 10 years as part of their final negotiations for the fiscal year 2027 National Defense Authorization Act. “The case for a long-term reauthorization has only grown more urgent,” they wrote. “Recent incidents have demonstrated that advanced AI systems can identify and exploit software vulnerabilities at machine speed, collapsing the window between the discovery of a weakness and its use in an attack.” “AI tools are also making sophisticated cyber capabilities cheaper, faster and easier to use, allowing threats to spread and adapt in real time,” they continued. “In this environment, the speed and breadth with which defenders share information determines whether they keep pace with adversaries. That speed depends on the legal certainty CISA 2015 provides.” The letter’s signatories include overarching business groups like the Chamber of Commerce and Business Roundtable, the latter of which led the letter, as well as groups representing critical infrastructure sectors such as aviation, telecommunications and technology. The House version of the fiscal 2027 defense bill includes a 10-year extension. The Senate version notably does not, and past efforts to include a long-term extension in the defense bill, which has been signed into law every year for decades, have encountered objections from Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky. Paul has hinged his support for any long-term extension of CISA 2015 on adoption of provisions designed to curtail past practices at the other CISA — the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency — that he maintains threaten free speech. Top Trump administration cyber officials have pressed Congress for a straightforward extension of the CISA 2015 laws. The Trump administration has also touted its efforts to crack down on what they said was the free-speech-limiting disinformation work of the agency CISA, which the Biden administration denied impinged on free speech and that it had ended anyway. The annual defense policy bill often passes at the end of each calendar year or beginning of the next. A potential congressional committee leadership shuffle could change the equation for CISA 2015 in 2027, but the Dec. 11 expiration looms in 2026.

articles.title: Snap Settles Landmark Trial Over Teen Mental Health
articles.content: Nov 2 (Reuters) - Snapchat parent Snap Inc SNAP.N has reached a settlement during a trial over claims brought by two teenagers who say the company designed the platform to be addictive, causing their depression, anxiety and eating disorders, attorneys for the plaintiffs said on Monday. By Reuters 2 Nov 2026 0 A person poses with the Snapchat logo displayed on a mobile phone in Liverpool, Britain, 23 January 2026. A proposal to ban under-16s from accessing social media in the UK will be considered in the House of Commons after peers in the House of Lords voted 261 to 150 in favour of an amendment to the Children’s Wellbeing and Schools Bill. If adopted, the amendment would require social media companies to implement strict and effective age checks in order to prevent underage users from signing up. EPA/ADAM VAUGHAN Dive Deeper Speed Read Listen Dive Deeper By Diana Novak Jones Jury selection began last week for the trial, the second in Los Angeles state court over claims brought by young people who say they became addicted to social media after Snap, Meta Platforms META.O, TikTok and Alphabet's GOOGL.O YouTube designed their platforms to encourage compulsive use. The plaintiffs had previously settled with Meta , TikTok and YouTube. "Our ultimate goal is to hold these social media companies accountable for how their actions have impacted millions of children across the country, and these settlements allow us to keep building toward that goal," John Morgan and Emily Jeffcott, trial attorneys for plaintiff K.D.B., said in a statement. The trial was set to be the first for Snap in the sweeping litigation over social media's impact on teens, after the company settled the other cases that had been scheduled for trial. The company's chief executive, Evan Spiegel, had been expected to testify. The case had been selected from thousands of pending lawsuits as a bellwether intended to test the claims against Snap and the other companies and potentially influence how similar cases are resolved. The next bellwether trials are scheduled to begin in March, according to the plaintiffs' lawyers. A Snap spokesperson said in a statement that the company has built safeguards, launched safety tutorials and partnered with experts, and remains committed to “continually strengthening the safety, privacy, and well-being of our community." Plaintiffs S.J., a 16-year-old girl from Illinois, and K.D.B., an 18-year-old from Mississippi, say they began using YouTube as early as age 3 and the other platforms around age 9, developing compulsive habits they blame on features such as autoplay and infinite scroll. The companies have rejected claims their platforms were designed to addict young people, and say they have taken action to make the apps safe places for young people to express themselves. Social media companies face thousands of lawsuits in federal and state courts brought by individuals, school districts, municipalities and other government entities alleging the companies knowingly sought to addict children to their platforms, contributing to a youth mental health crisis involving anxiety, depression and suicide. In the first case to go to trial, which ended in March, a Los Angeles jury found Meta and YouTube had been negligent and awarded a young woman $6 million in damages . The next two teens whose cases were selected for trials either settled or dropped their claims against the companies. The first school district chosen for trial settled with all of the companies. In August, Meta struck settlements worth up to $18 billion with nearly every state and US territory to resolve lawsuits brought by attorneys general over claims its platforms harmed teens and agreed to make changes to how Instagram and Facebook work for teens. The deal conditioned $5 billion of the payout on the states reaching similar settlements with Snap, TikTok and YouTube. (Reporting by Diana Novak Jones in Chicago, Editing by Alexia Garamfalvi and Matthew Lewis) World

articles.title: Enterprise Tech Rejects Token Counts for Working Software Metrics
articles.content: Provided by HPE When a developer gives an AI agent a coding task, the agent does more than answer once. It plans, generates code, runs tests, and repeats the process to correct errors. A single task can use 10 to 50 times more tokens than a basic chat prompt. The more useful the agent becomes, the more calls it makes. With per-token pricing, the workflows creating the most value can also become the most expensive. The financial pressure is already visible. Uber reportedly exhausted its entire 2026 AI budget by April after expanding its use of Claude Code. GitHub Copilot moved from flat-rate pricing to metered credits. Gartner predicts that AI coding token costs will surpass average developer salaries by 2028. The natural response is rationing usage caps, seat limits, and approvals before developers launch agents. But blanket limits can restrict the workflows delivering value. They also optimize the wrong number. Cost per token measures consumption, not results. Some spending reflects waste, including retries and runaway loops. Some represents the work of shipping software. A meter cannot distinguish them, and neither can a spending cap. A better measure is cost per merged pull request: total AI-assisted development cost divided by the number of changes that pass review and are merged. Track rework and defects alongside it so cheaper changes do not conceal lower quality. If that cost falls as AI usage rises, without compromising quality, developers are converting more consumption into useful software. The question is not how many tokens they use, but how much finished work the investment produces. Improving that equation requires two changes: reserve expensive inference for tasks that need it, and lower the cost of routine work. Agentic coding does not require the most powerful model at every step. Use a frontier model, or an on-premises flagship when policy requires it, for difficult planning and novel reasoning. Route suitable work, including code generation, test creation, and repeated refactoring, to open-weight models you operate yourself. A gateway can route requests according to task complexity, data sensitivity, cost, and latency. This reserves premium inference for the moments that justify it rather than applying premium pricing to an entire workflow. Meter the exception, not the workload. Open-weight models make this division increasingly practical. Software-engineering benchmarks show that leading open-weight models can approach frontier performance on some tasks. That does not establish equivalence across every repository or workflow. Evaluate candidates against your own code, tests, and acceptance criteria before assigning production work. Next, decide who owns the capacity. With rented inference, every call adds to the bill. With owned capacity, most of the cost is committed upfront, so each additional call gets cheaper as usage grows. The economics are simple: per-token pricing makes heavy use more expensive, while owned capacity becomes more efficient as teams use it more. Ownership is not free, though. Power, operations, maintenance, and depreciation all must be considered. The number that matters is the fully loaded cost per merged pull request. Owned capacity also delivers a type of value that never appears on an invoice: control over sensitive code. When code generation and testing run on-premises, proprietary code stays inside the enterprise. Only approved planning prompts and governed exceptions go to external models, through a gateway the organization controls. That opens the sensitive repositories where security usually stalls adoption, and where the biggest gains are waiting. At HPE, a hybrid AI platform routes routine workloads from more than 150 internal applications to open-weight models running on premises, including on HPE Private Cloud AI. The result: token costs down 30 to 50%. That is the point of hybrid. With HPE Private Cloud AI, owning your inference does not mean giving up frontier models. Run the volume on capacity you own and let a gateway send the hardest work. Data also shows that usage, not licensed headcount, drives spend. The top 5% of users generated most of the consumption, and the heaviest used roughly 450 times more than the lightest on the same license. If power users grow from a small minority to half the workforce, monthly spend can rise about 4.4 times with flat headcount. Your mix will differ, which is exactly why you need to measure it. HPE tracks two metrics and recommends customers do the same. First, it tracks cost per active developer, because averaging across all licenses hides the power users driving spend. Second, it tracks cost per merged pull request, because it connects AI spending to software that ships. Baseline both costs before changing infrastructure. Then run a complete development cycle on owned capacity. If both metrics do not improve as usage grows, your current model may still be the better choice. Owned capacity is not for everyone. Low or unpredictable usage favors APIs, with no capital tied up in idle infrastructure. Ownership pays off when sustained demand keeps it busy. Most enterprises will run hybrid: frontier APIs for demanding or intermittent work, owned capacity for repeatable volume. A governed gateway decides what leaves the building, so you get frontier models without giving up sovereignty over your code. As developers lean harder on coding agents, usage will keep rising. The real choice is whether that growth shows up as a bigger variable-cost bill or as more software shipped on capacity you own. The companies that lead AI-assisted development will not ration adoption to control costs. They will build an operating model where more AI use improves the economics instead of undermining them. articles.content: Access a copy of the Lumen Database PDF listing the disputed URLs: [ pdf ] Hostinger, a global web hosting and domain registration provider, briefly suspended journalist and documentary filmmaker, Paranjoy Guha Thakurta’s website ( http://www.paranjoy.in/ ) and the domains linked to it on October 28, and later restored them on November 2, according to the Guha’s posts on X. The now-restored websites documents and archives 12 years of his work in journalism, books, documentary films and music videos. These were the affected domain and subdomains (now accessible):  https://www.paranjoy.in/ https://media.paranjoy.in/ https://adanifiles.paranjoy.in/ “Backdoor censorship through web hosting providers sets a dangerous precedent for the independence of the media and freedom of expression,” read Guha’s public statement. He also said that his legal team is preparing to challenge the October 24 order and the suspension of his website. The restoration happened after his post went viral and drew public criticism. The website is now accessible. What is the rationale behind the Hostinger takedown: The suspension reportedly came four days after a Delhi court passed an ex parte order, which is generally passed without hearing the other side, against a single NewsClick.in article on his website. However, Hostinger did not cite that order, according to Guha Thakurta. He said the company gave an abuse report for “Fraud/Scam” as the reason. When Guha’s colleague contacted Hostinger support at 6:48 AM on October 28, a hosting specialist said the suspension followed that abuse report and that “unsuspension is not negotiable in this case”, Guha Thakurta said. He said Hostinger gave no prior notice or chance to respond. Guha Thakurta disputed the ‘fraud’ label: Guha Thakurta said checks on October 28 contradict the abuse report. VirusTotal showed zero of 92 security vendors flagging paranjoy.in or media.paranjoy.in as malicious or fraudulent, he said, and categorised it under “news and media”. Google Safe Browsing returned “No unsafe content found” for paranjoy.in and adanifiles.paranjoy.in. He argued that even where a court directs removal of one URL, a host has no justification to suspend an entire domain without notice. He has asked Hostinger four questions: Who filed the abuse report, and when was it received? What verification did the abuse team conduct before classifying the site as “Fraud/Scam”? Why was no notice or copy of the complaint sent before suspension? On what basis did the specialist call the suspension “not negotiable”? A brief list of sequences in Guha’s case is just before the end of this article.  What we dont know: The text of the October 24 order has not been made public, so it is unclear whether it covers hosting providers. It is also unclear who filed the abuse report with Hostinger, whether Hostinger acted on it or the court order, and whether the site has been restored. We have emailed Hostinger seeking clarification in this, we will update the article if we hear back.  52 URLs on the takedown list: The complaint to Google, recorded in the Lumen Database (Notice ID 101001876), targeted 52 URLs, Guha Thakurta said. These included reports from the Caravan Magazine, The Economic Times, Business Standard, The Caravan, Mint, NDTV Profit and The Quint, as well as posts on X, Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn and Scribd. A full list of the URLs extracted from the Lumen database is at the end of this article.  Most of these remain accessible, he said. Item 39 on the list is the original NewsClick article , which he said was still live at the time of his statement. The NewsClick article remains accessible even at the time of writing this article. Moreover, Journalist Sucheta Dalal said that MoneyWise publication were also served with “same order.” Thanking Internet Freedom Foundation, she noted that when they challenged the order, the court ruled that “the defamation suit will no longer proceed against Moneywise Media LLP.” Read more about this case here . A few public reactions to takedown of Guha’s website:  One disputed news article can’t justify the takedown of a 12-year-old body of work: “What a dangerous precedent! A court order concerning a specific article cannot become a pretext for wiping out an entire 12-year archive built by Paranjoy. This shouldn’t go unchallenged! In solidarity,” wrote Neha Bora on X. Legal notices are being used to make work vanish: Journalist Ravish Kumar said “post deletion has reached a whole new level” and that “the entire website has been made to disappear”, in a post translated into English. He said the internet had fallen into the clutches of a “law mafia” that uses notices to erase people’s work. “Freedom of expression, freedom of the press is being extinguished at every level,” he said. Taking down a host domain without notice is “a new low”: YouTuber and political commentator Akash Banerjee said assaults, court cases and account takedowns against journalists have become routine. He asked how “12 years of work” could be “wiped out because some moneybags filed a case”. Users should move away from Hostinger: Fact-checker Pratik Sinha called for a boycott of Hostinger and urged its users to switch. He named 1984, Gandi and Njalla as more censorship-resistant providers and offered to help people migrate. Erasing decades of work “is a crime”: Journalist Ajit Anjum said wiping out a senior journalist’s work “in one stroke” is no small matter. He alleged a “planned conspiracy” to suppress voices that expose those in power and the businesses they nurture. From John Doe orders to deleting a whole website: Journalist Abhisar Sharma called the takedown “unfair and illegal”. He pointed to John Doe orders, which name unidentified defendants and which influential businessmen use to remove content against them, and asked how it had come to removing an entire website. Takedown tactics are spreading from platforms to publishing: Journalist Pankaj Pachauri , a former communications adviser in the Prime Minister’s Office, said “takedown tactics” are moving from social media platforms to online publishing. He said most domain providers have no India office or address for legal redress, and that courts need to be sensitised to this. More responses are here . Keep backups, and avoid .in domains: Responding to the same, MediaNama founder and editor Nikhil Pahwa shared advice for people running websites and social media accounts: Export social media history regularly and keep offline copies, so an archive can be hosted on your own site if an account is blocked. Avoid .in domains, citing changing policies at the National Internet Exchange of India (NIXI), and avoid Indian registrars and very popular ones. Register backup domains for your keyword. Keep a backup server with another host and back up deployments, so the site can go live again. NIXI’s suspension of ChaloSansad.in domain: During the Jantar Matar Protests in July 2026 seeking the resignation of ex-Union Education Minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, NIXI, India’s .IN domain registry, suspended the website, chalosansad.in citing the invalid WHOIS contact details. When Viswanathan, the owner of chalosansad.in ,  submitted his redacted Aadhaar identity details, NIXI then reasoned that the word “Sansad” is exclusive to the government under the Emblems and Names (Prevention of Improper Use) Act, 1950.This case is being heard in the Delhi HC now , with the next hearing scheduled for January 27, 2027. In July 2025, NIXI mandated the Know Your Customer (KYC) verification of the users, which can be completed using MeitY’s DigiLocker app. If any foreign nationals have .in domain, they’ll have to complete their KYC verification through submitting ‘their passport, driving license, a letter issued by the Foreign Embassy or Mission of India, and income tax returns for the last two years,’ MediaNama reported when this change was announced.  “I don’t think NIXI is fit as a registrar for the .in domain. They’re seeking to enforce KYC via India’s digilocker for domain registration, and disallowing the registration/renewal of .in domain names to foreign citizens. This is a regressive move, not the first from NIXi, and goes against the spirit of the way the internet is structured: anyone can create a website on the internet and register a domain with any registrar. This move transforms NIXI from being an enabler to a bottleneck. Classic redtape-ism from a bureaucracy. Does NIXI have any clarity on what % of .in domains are used by cybercriminals? They’re throwing out the baby with the bathwater.” – Nikhil Pahwa, Medianama editor,  A brief sequence of events in Paranjoy Guha’s case: September 30, 2019: NewsClick publishes the article, “The Maze of Political Links of Indiabull’s Sameer Gehlaut”. March 11, 2020: Indiabulls Housing Finance Limited files a criminal defamation complaint (CC No. 1765/2020) at Patiala House Courts, New Delhi. The accused are NewsClick, Reader’s Editor Urmilesh, co-author Sourodipto Sanyal, editor Prabir Purkayastha and Paranjoy Guha Thakurta. June 6, 2025: A magistrate drops proceedings against Purkayastha. The other four are summoned under Sections 499 and 500 of the Indian Penal Code, which cover defamation. The formal summons, issued July 9, 2025, sets an appearance for July 30, 2025. August 27, 2026: Legal counsel for Indiabulls founder Sameer Gehlaut sends a legal notice demanding takedown within 24 to 48 hours. The notice claims an Economic Offences Wing (EOW) status report changed the factual position. Guha Thakurta’s counsel replies on September 2. October 24, 2026: Indiabulls Nests Limited and Gehlaut obtain an ex parte ad interim injunction in Civil Suit No. 529/2026 ( Indiabulls Nests Ltd. & Anr. v. Ashok Kumar/John Doe & Ors. ). Guha Thakurta is Defendant No. 19. The order directs removal and de-indexing of his article, listed as Item A-33 in Schedule A. October 25, 2026: The plaintiffs’ advocates email him the order and demand deletion and written confirmation of compliance. October 26, 2026: Gehlaut emails him directly, threatening to move court under Order XXXIX Rule 2A of the Code of Civil Procedure, which deals with disobeying an injunction. He notes the next hearing is on December 18, 2026. The same day, Gehlaut’s advocates file a court-order takedown complaint with Google. October 28, 2026: Google Search Console notifies Guha Thakurta that it is blocking the article’s URL that is in paranjoy.in from google’s search results and Google.co.in. articles.title: Election Authorities Prepare Synthetic Generative Stickers for 2026 Midterms
articles.content: • Voting in 2026 Is Getting an AI Slop 'I Voted' Sticker · Nov 2, 2026 at 11:33 AM My polling place was handing out AI slop to midterm voters. It’s a small pleasure, but receiving an “I Voted” sticker after casting my ballot is one of my favorite parts of the whole voting process. I slap the sticker on my chest and spend the rest of the day feeling like I accomplished a little something. I participated in democracy and everyone who sees me will know it. Artificial intelligence robbed me of that small joy this year and replaced it with a small horror. My “I Voted” sticker is AI-generated slop.  Getting a little sticker when you vote has been a tradition in the US since the 1980s . It’s a symbol of the election cycle. People take selfies and post them or share them with friends. It’s a celebration of democracy and a small way to pressure people into going to the ballot box.  The voting sticker has been subject to every kind of discourse imaginable. Are “I Voted” stickers worth the cost? Wondered Marketplace in 2020. A cemetery in New York has spent time and money tending to the grave of Susan B Anthony because voters coat it in stickers during voting season. In 2008, companies like Starbucks and Ben and Jerry’s ran afoul of election laws for offering free treats to people who showed their “I Voted” stickers. It’s appropriate but depressing that I got an AI slop “I Voted” sticker in 2026, the year it feels like the mainstream began to reckon with AI. My sticker is ugly. It’s a busy circular nightmare. “I Voted” is spelled out in small bronze text at the top of the ring. Bronze laurels encircle a bronze bald eagle that stretches atop the American flag. Below this is more text: “250 YEARS ANNIVERSARY” and "SEMIQUENCENTENNIAL.” Below that, another line reads — as best I can tell — “CEKEVPATIVG EDELDOA.” I assume this was meant to say “CELEBRATING FREEDOM," but whoever churned out this slop wasn’t using the latest models and the fine detail is lost. I put the sticker on reluctantly, but I was not proud. I sent a photo of the offending sticker to journalist friends with my face cropped out. They immediately noticed it was AI-generated. I did not post my sticker online. I shared it with no one else. My democratic joy turned to shame. A few hours later, a friend sent me a selfie. He’d just left the voting booth. His sticker was beautiful, tasteful, a testament to the subtle art of the “I Voted” sticker. A red ring enclosed a blue field. The crescent and palmetto (symbols of South Carolina) sat elegantly behind a bold white “I VOTED.” His sticker catches the eye. Passers-by will know exactly what the sticker says. They know he voted. Anyone looking at my sticker will wonder how I spilled some bronze paint on my chest. I trembled with indignation. One town over from me they’re giving out the good stickers and I’m stuck with slop. First my town of 12,000 installs 33 Flock cameras and now this?  I spent some time scrolling through social media to see other “I Voted” stickers. So many are so beautiful. Michigan runs a contest where students can submit their own idea for a sticker and the state will print up the winners . Kentucky , Albany , and several other places around the country do the same. Louisiana commissions local artists to produce gorgeous stickers . My mouth hung up in a jealous scowl as I stared at pictures of New Orleanians bedecked with a sticker showing a hand drawn trumpet blasting out “I Voted” alongside Mardi Gras beads. Only Denton, Texas (another place I’ve lived, weirdly) seems to also have AI-generated slop stickers . Denton’s sticker is, at least, personalized. The city’s court house is in the corner looking more or less correct. The “I Voted” is large and centered in the sticker itself. Like mine, the image is too busy. Too much text, too many fireworks, and the inclusion of the Liberty Bell clutters the whole thing up. The central message — “I Voted” — is bright white. It doesn’t sink into a busy bronze soup like on my sticker. Complaining about AI-slop “I Voted” stickers may seem trivial in a world where AIs are choosing targets in warzones and vibecoders are reverse-engineering every piece of software ever written. But these little things are important. These small annoyances pile up until things like ChatGPT flyers are so ubiquitous that you don’t notice them anymore. The AI drive-thru works well enough and one day you stop worrying about it so much. You get an ugly AI slop “I Voted” sticker and you slap it on or toss it out. Enough of these build up until you don’t notice that AI all around you. And then, one day, it’s all normal. Right now we’re figuring out where our AI lines are. Society is negotiating what the future will look like. We’re fighting data centers , figuring out how to burn tokens to keep our bosses happy, and learning what we will and won’t abide. Me? I draw the line at AI-generated “I Voted” stickers. Matthew Gault is a writer covering weird tech, nuclear war, and video games. He’s worked for Reuters, Motherboard, and the New York Times. articles.content: Add TT as Preferred Source Taiwan’s manufacturing sector continued to expand strongly last month, buoyed by robust artificial intelligence (AI)-related demand, although shortages of key components are delaying some AI server shipments, the Chung-Hua Institution for Economic Research (CIER, 中華經濟研究院) said yesterday. The manufacturing purchasing managers’ index (PMI) eased to 62.5 from 63.4 a month earlier, while the non-manufacturing index (NMI) fell to 55.4 from 56.9. Both remained well above the 50-point threshold separating expansion from contraction, indicating that business activity continued to grow, the CIER said. CIER president Lien Hsien-ming (連賢明) said the manufacturing sector remained on a solid growth path, with AI-related demand continuing to support production and orders. However, supply constraints involving key raw materials and components have become a growing obstacle, preventing some manufacturers from shipping products as scheduled, he said. The problem is particularly evident in AI servers, which require a large number of components to be assembled into a finished product. A delay in obtaining even one critical component can hold up the entire production process, Lien said. Memory chips are not the only bottleneck, as substrates have also become increasingly difficult to secure, he said. Substrate production is constrained by limited capacity, while some upstream materials are sourced from Japan, making the supply chain vulnerable to disruptions at multiple stages, he added. The CIER’s survey showed that the new orders index remained robust at 63.2 last month, indicating continued growth in demand. However, the backlog of orders index fell to 53.9, its slowest expansion since January, amid continuing production and delivery difficulties, the CIER said. Meanwhile, the supplier delivery times and raw material prices indices remained near 70, reflecting longer delivery times and persistent cost pressures as companies compete for increasingly scarce supplies, it said. Asked whether the simultaneous declines in the PMI and NMI signaled that the economy had peaked, Lien said it was too early to draw such a conclusion. Both PMI and NMI measure changes in business activity from the previous month, rather than the overall level of activity, Lien said. As both remained above 50, the readings indicated continued expansion, not an economic downturn, he said. Lien also cautioned against assuming that the AI industry could sustain its current growth pace indefinitely. As production capacity expands and the industry’s base becomes larger, maintaining annual capacity growth of 20 percent to 30 percent will become increasingly challenging, he said. Nevertheless, manufacturers remain optimistic about their business outlook, as the six-month business outlook index rose to 61.7 last month, staying above 60 for the 10th consecutive month. The services-oriented NMI also registered its 20th consecutive month of expansion, although at a slower pace, Lien said. Travel fairs, department store anniversary sales and major online shopping festivals this month are expected to boost retail, hotel and restaurant sales, he said.
